The first regression prints a warning about an essentially perfect fit. That is correct rather than broken: number_range_b is exactly 2 times number_range_a, so the fitted slope is 0.5 and the residuals are zero to rounding error.

Answer

Rewrite the code above across as many chunks as you think it needs, with a comment at the top of each saying what stage it covers.

3. A First Look at ggplot2

Every figure so far has been built with ggplot2, one of the packages tidyverse loads. Next workshop leans on it heavily, so it is worth taking the pieces apart now.

The name is short for “grammar of graphics”. The idea is that a statistical graphic is not a chart type you pick off a menu but a sentence you assemble out of a few standard parts:

  • data: a data frame, one row per observation.
  • aesthetic mappings: which column controls which visual property, written inside aes(). Position on the x axis, position on the y axis, color, fill, shape and size are all aesthetics.
  • geoms: the marks actually drawn. geom_point() draws points, geom_line() lines, geom_col() bars, geom_histogram() a histogram.
  • everything else: scales, facets, labels, theme.

Layers are joined with + at the end of the line, never at the start of the next one. R has to see an incomplete expression to know that more is coming.

The data below is invented for the sake of the example. It is not real market data and should not be quoted as such. Six years, two crops, one price per crop per year.

farm_prices <- data.frame(
  # rep(..., times = 2) repeats the whole sequence twice
  year  = rep(2018:2023, times = 2),
  # rep(..., each = 6) repeats each label six times in a row
  crop  = rep(c("Wheat", "Canola"), each = 6),
  price = c(230, 245, 260, 315, 340, 300,
            480, 505, 540, 720, 815, 690)
)

# str() gives a compact description of any object: type, size, and the first values
str(farm_prices)
## 'data.frame':    12 obs. of  3 variables:
##  $ year : int  2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2018 2019 2020 2021 ...
##  $ crop : chr  "Wheat" "Wheat" "Wheat" "Wheat" ...
##  $ price: num  230 245 260 315 340 300 480 505 540 720 ...

Twelve rows and three columns: year is an integer, crop is character, price is a double. This shape, one row per observation with variables in columns, is what ggplot2 expects, and getting data into it is most of what the next workshop is about.

Start with the first two parts and nothing else. ggplot() takes the data as its first argument and the mappings as its second, and the mappings are written inside aes().

ggplot(data = farm_prices, mapping = aes(x = year, y = price)) +
  labs(
    title = "Data and mappings, but no geom",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Price (invented dollars per tonne)"
  )

An empty panel. The axes are there, and the y axis is already scaled to cover the price column, which runs from 230 to 815, because ggplot read the data and worked out the range it needs. What is missing is any instruction about what to draw. That is the geom’s job.

Add one layer and the points appear. The arguments data = and mapping = are almost always dropped, since they are the first two by position, so from here on the call is just ggplot(farm_prices, aes(...)).

ggplot(farm_prices, aes(x = year, y = price)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "One geom added",
    subtitle = "Twelve points, one per row of farm_prices",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Price (invented dollars per tonne)"
  )

Twelve points, one per row, in two obvious clusters. Nothing in the plot says which cluster is which, because nothing has been mapped to a visual property that could tell them apart. Mapping crop to color fixes that, and ggplot builds the legend on its own.

Note where the mapping goes. Anything inside aes() is driven by a column of the data. Anything outside aes(), such as linewidth = 1 here, is a fixed setting applied to the whole layer.

ggplot(farm_prices, aes(x = year, y = price, color = crop)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  # force a tick at every year rather than every second one
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2018:2023) +
  labs(
    title = "Mapping crop to color splits the data into two series",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Price (invented dollars per tonne)",
    color = "Crop"   # names the legend
  )

Two lines with points on them, one per crop, and a legend naming them. The color mapping did three jobs at once: it split each geom into two groups, assigned a color to each, and generated the legend. Both crops rise to a 2022 peak and fall back in 2023, canola from a much higher base.

The mapping and setting distinction catches everyone once. Putting a literal color inside aes() tells ggplot that "blue" is data, so it creates a grouping with one level, picks its own color for that level, and adds a legend for it.

# WRONG: "blue" is treated as data, so the points are not blue
ggplot(farm_prices, aes(x = year, y = price, color = "blue")) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "color inside aes() is read as data", x = "Year", y = "Price")

# RIGHT: outside aes(), "blue" is a setting applied to the layer
ggplot(farm_prices, aes(x = year, y = price)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "blue") +
  labs(title = "color outside aes() is a fixed setting", x = "Year", y = "Price")

The first plot has salmon-colored points and a legend titled “colour” whose single entry reads “blue”. The second has blue points and no legend. Inside aes() means “look this up in the data”; outside means “just do this”.

Facets are the other way to split data, giving each group its own panel instead of its own color. scales = "free_y" lets each panel choose its own y axis, which is right when the groups live on different scales and wrong when you want them compared directly.

ggplot(farm_prices, aes(x = year, y = price)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ crop, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2018:2023) +
  labs(
    title = "The same data as bars, one panel per crop",
    subtitle = "Each panel gets its own y axis because scales = 'free_y'",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Price (invented dollars per tonne)"
  )

Each panel now has its own axis, so both crops fill their space and the shape of each series is easy to read. The cost is that the bars are no longer comparable across panels: the tallest canola bar is more than twice the tallest wheat bar, and nothing on the page says so. Drop scales = "free_y" when that comparison is the point.

Bars have one more setting worth knowing before Day 2. When two groups share an x value, geom_col() stacks them on top of each other by default, because position = "stack" is the default. For prices that is nonsense: the top of a stacked bar is a wheat price added to a canola price, a number that means nothing.

# the default, and wrong for this data: bar heights are the two prices added together
ggplot(farm_prices, aes(x = factor(year), y = price, fill = crop)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Stacked bars, the default",
    subtitle = "The top of each bar is wheat plus canola, which is not a price",
    x = "Year", y = "Price (invented dollars per tonne)", fill = "Crop"
  )

# position = "dodge" puts the groups side by side instead of on top of each other
ggplot(farm_prices, aes(x = factor(year), y = price, fill = crop)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Dodged bars",
    subtitle = "Two bars per year, each one an actual price",
    x = "Year", y = "Price (invented dollars per tonne)", fill = "Crop"
  )

In the first figure the 2022 bar reaches past 1150, a number that appears nowhere in the data. In the second, the same year shows two bars at 340 and 815, both of which are real. Stacking is right for parts of a whole, such as area planted by crop, and wrong for anything that should not be added together.

Note that x = factor(year) replaced x = year in these two. Bars want a discrete axis, and wrapping the numeric year in factor() gives them one, with a slot per year.

Some geoms do not plot a column directly but compute something from it first. geom_histogram() takes one continuous variable, cuts its range into bins, counts how many observations land in each, and draws the counts. That is why only x is mapped here and the y axis appears from nowhere.

# set.seed() fixes the random draw so this figure is the same every time it runs
set.seed(2026)

# 200 invented field yields in tonnes per hectare
yields <- data.frame(yield = rnorm(200, mean = 4.2, sd = 0.6))

ggplot(yields, aes(x = yield)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "grey40", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of 200 simulated field yields",
    subtitle = "geom_histogram() counts observations per bin; the y axis is computed, not mapped",
    x = "Yield (tonnes per hectare)",
    y = "Number of fields"
  )

A roughly bell-shaped pile centered a little above 4, with essentially everything between 2.7 and 5.8, which is what rnorm() with a mean of 4.2 and a standard deviation of 0.6 should produce. Change bins and the picture changes, so always say what you used.

Four errors account for most of the time people lose to ggplot2 in their first week.

  • Joining layers with %>% instead of +. The pipe is for data, + is for plot layers. Next workshop uses both in the same line and the difference matters.
  • Putting the + at the start of the next line rather than the end of the current one. R finishes the statement at the line break and then meets a + with nothing in front of it.
  • Forgetting aes(), as in ggplot(farm_prices, x = year). Columns have to be mapped inside aes() or ggplot never looks in the data for them.
  • Mapping a constant, as in color = "blue" inside aes(). Settings go outside.

Three habits to carry into the next workshop. Label every axis and give every plot a title, since an unlabeled chart is unreadable to anyone but its author. Build plots one layer at a time and look at the result after each +, which is far faster than debugging ten layers at once. And save with ggsave("filename.png", width = 7, height = 4.5), which writes the last plot drawn to a file at a size you control.

Conclusion

Today we’ve revisited some old topics, and introduced some new ones.

In Section 1, we reviewed our main data structures (1.1) and methods for control flow in R programming (1.2).

In Section 2, we discussed ways to make sure our code is easy to understand (2.1, 2.3, 2.6) and work with (2.2, 2.4), and some ways to just make everyone’s life easier (2.5). Do your best to follow these, and you’ll have an easier time in the long run, and anyone else reading your code (cough cough, the Course Assistants marking it!) will have a much happier time.

Section 3 introduced ggplot2, where a plot is a data frame plus a set of aesthetic mappings plus one or more geoms, stacked with +.

Next time, we’ll move on and introduce some new industry-standard packages for really getting our hands dirty and working with data.

Extra Practice

Exercise 1: Write R code to reverse an array, taking the array from user input.

Input:  10, 12, 13, 14, 15
Output: 15, 14, 13, 12, 10

The solution below builds the reversed vector by hand to show the mechanics. numeric(n) creates an empty numeric vector of length n to write into, the loop counter i walks the input backwards with n:1, and a second counter j walks the output forwards from 1. Base R has rev(), which does the whole job in one call; write the loop first, then check yourself against rev(input_array).

# readline() prompts you when you run this chunk in RStudio.
# There is no console when the notebook is knitted, so fall back to the example values.
if (interactive()) {
  n <- as.numeric(readline(prompt = "Enter the size of the array: "))
  input_array <- numeric(n)

  # take user input for the array elements
  for (i in 1:n) {
    input_array[i] <- as.numeric(readline())
  }
} else {
  input_array <- c(10, 12, 13, 14, 15)
  n <- length(input_array)
}

rev_array <- numeric(n)

j <- 1
for (i in n:1) {
  rev_array[j] <- input_array[i]
  j <- j + 1
}

print(input_array)
## [1] 10 12 13 14 15
print(rev_array)
## [1] 15 14 13 12 10

The second printed line is the first one backwards. Note that i counts down while j counts up; getting those two straight is the whole exercise.

Exercise 2: Write R code that defines a function called factorial_func() and use it to calculate the factorial of a number given by the user.

Input:  5
Output: 120

The accumulator here starts at 1 rather than 0, because the loop multiplies instead of adding and anything times zero stays zero. One caution: 1:num counts downward when num is 0, giving 1 0, so this version returns 0 for an input of 0 rather than the correct 1. Guarding against that is a good use of an if statement.

# factorial

factorial_func <- function(num) {
  result <- 1

  for (i in 1:num) {
    result <- result * i
  }

  return(result)
}

# readline() prompts you when you run this chunk in RStudio.
# There is no console when the notebook is knitted, so fall back to a fixed value.
n <- if (interactive()) as.numeric(readline(prompt = "Enter a number: ")) else 5

print(paste("Factorial of", n, "is", factorial_func(n)))
## [1] "Factorial of 5 is 120"

Factorials get large fast, which is easier to appreciate on a chart than in a column of numbers. The loop below calls factorial_func() on 1 through 10 and stores each result.

fact_df <- data.frame(n = 1:10, result = numeric(10))

for (k in 1:10) {
  fact_df$result[k] <- factorial_func(k)
}

fact_df
ggplot(fact_df, aes(x = n, y = result)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(color = "darkred", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  # a log y axis compresses the huge values so the small ones stay visible
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "factorial_func() from 1 to 10, on a log scale",
    subtitle = "1! is 1 and 10! is 3628800, so a linear y axis would show almost nothing",
    x = "n",
    y = "n factorial (log scale)"
  )

On a log axis the points climb steadily rather than shooting off the top, which is what a log scale is for: it makes multiplicative growth readable. Try the same plot without scale_y_log10() and the first eight points flatten onto the axis.
